planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted hardwood cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Afghanistan is grown as much for its showy, semi-double, brick-red spring flowers as for its fruit, and needs no second tree for pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates handle heavy clay and alkaline conditions better than most fruiting trees once roots are established. Afghanistan is a vigorous, heavy-blooming pomegranate selection grown in home orchards as much for its dense flush of large, ruffled, semi-double red-orange spring flowers as for its fruit, making it one of the more ornamental fruiting cultivars available. The medium fruit ripens to a deep red rind enclosing garnet-colored arils with a rich, wine-like, tart-sweet flavor and firmer seeds than soft-seeded types, suited to juicing as much as fresh eating. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and tend toward a naturally dense, twiggy, multi-stemmed shrub form; prune lightly to open the canopy and remove root suckers, since fruit forms on new growth.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted hardwood cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Ambrosia is prized for producing some of the largest fruit of any pomegranate cultivar, often exceeding a pound each. Self-fertile; no cross-pollination needed.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate clay, sand, and alkaline soils better than most fruiting trees once established. Ambrosia is a French heirloom pomegranate selected for its exceptionally large fruit, sometimes approaching softball size and well over a pound, with pale pink-blushed skin and mild, low-acid, sweet arils that are gentler and less tart than Wonderful. The large fruit size makes Ambrosia a favorite for fresh eating and for show, though the thinner-flavored juice is less concentrated than smaller, more intensely flavored cultivars. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and benefit from thinning excess fruit to prevent limb breakage and splitting from the sheer weight of the oversized crop; prune lightly each year to encourage new fruiting wood.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

common_name: Nana Dwarf Pomegranate (Compact Ornamental Fruiting Pomegranate)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Nana stays under 3 feet, so it is equally at home as a foundation shrub, container specimen, or informal low hedge and needs no cross-pollinator.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; this dwarf pomegranate is far more tolerant of poor, dry, and alkaline soils than most flowering shrubs of similar size. Nana is a naturally compact, densely branched pomegranate selection that reaches only 2-3 feet tall and wide, retaining the species' narrow, glossy foliage and bright orange-red, trumpet-shaped flowers borne over a long summer season, followed by small, tart, seedy fruit that is edible but grown mainly for ornament rather than harvest. Its small mature size makes it useful in foundation plantings, rock gardens, low informal hedges, and containers or bonsai culture where a full-size pomegranate tree would be unmanageable. Established plants shrug off heat and drought and need only an occasional light shaping prune, since like all pomegranates it flowers and fruits on new wood.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Punica granatum
